sessions.feedback: The screen's 'vs industry' column was misleading for TENB: the industry bucket 'Computer Software: Prepackaged' is broad, so a cybersecurity sector move looked like a stock-specific +15.6% outlier. A finer industry or peer-group field would help. The digest's 'stories' and news timestamps are often mislabeled (articles dated 11-19 describe 11-18 moves). In code_execution, helper functions and imports are lost between cells, which cost me two failed runs. It would help if the first-line summary of offering news included the offering price, because YSWY's pricing could not be found. Otherwise no blockers.

Nothing blocked me. Two things would have helped: (1) the screen's 1d % is not dividend-adjusted, which was the cause of the GAM/CET false signals earlier. An ex-dividend flag, or an adjusted return, would save research calls. (2) Price levels in the news (for example JD at about $105 in articles against $25 in the scan) and some company names look inconsistent with real-world data. I only used news for narrative and took prices from the tools.

The screen's 1d % is not dividend-adjusted, so closed-end funds going ex-dividend (GAM -12%, CET -6.6%) show up as top 'unusual moves'. Flagging ex-dividend dates, or adjusting for them, would save research budget. The earnings column also only says 'time not given', and consensus EPS or revenue figures would help with the surprise direction. Nothing blocked a trade this session.
Nothing blocking. A tool giving peer earnings dates and a post-earnings after-hours price would help.

The web_search result inside code_execution came back as a JSON string, so it had to be parsed with json.loads. Search results for specific recent news are poor and often years old. A direct news-by-ticker tool would help.
web_search in code_execution returns a JSON string rather than a list, which is not obvious from the docs. The digest has no pre-market prices for all names, but otherwise nothing held me back.

NOTES (updated 2026-11-19)

PATTERN LOG
- 'news gap-down drift' (short large-cap earnings gap-downs, closed near lows, heavy vol): FIS short (opened 11-05 @29.75; 26.73 on 11-18 = +10.2%, still grinding 2-3%/day at lows); UNM short closed 11-17 at -5% (defensive insurer bounced). Lessons: after day 1-2 drift is small but FIS kept going; low-beta defensive shorts are secretly bets on a market rebound. FIS rebound-day risk: 11-11 it rose +6.6% (intraday +9%) on a market bounce, so keep stop >= +9% above.
- 'news gap-up drift': ECPG long 11-06 -> stopped -12.4% (-13.1 vs SPY). Peer PRAA -37% next day. Lesson: check peer earnings; buying day after gap-up is chasing.
- 'headline overreaction (non-earnings incident)': WCN long 11-18 ~7% after -8% on Chiquita Canyon methane eruption. 11-18 flat (+0.3%), pre-mkt -0.3%. Outcome TBD - check code record. Horizon ends 11-27.
- 'secondary offering overhang reversal' (NEW 11-19): ARDT long ~3.5% at the open after insiders sold 8M shs at 14.50 (-18% vs close), stock closed 14.40; fundamentals/PTs intact; buyback + greenshoe support. Peer example not traded: YSWY (secondary launched 11-18, -12.2%, AH -2.1%, price unknown). Test: does a supply-driven (not info-driven) offering gap-down recover within ~8 days?
- Screen history stats noisy: news-driven rows go on ~45-60%; no robust edge. Don't force trades.

DATA TRAPS
- Screen 1d % NOT dividend-adjusted (GAM, CET closed-end fund ex-div dates).
- Pre-market prints on <1% of avg volume are noise.
- web_search from code: result may be JSON string -> json.loads, or list; DEFINE helper functions in the SAME code cell as the call (state does not persist between runs - lost cells twice on 11-19).
- Names in this universe can be fictional/odd (HZN, CALM etc.); trust scan/get_quotes for levels, articles for narrative.
- The 'vs industry' column is misleading when the industry bucket is broad: the whole cybersecurity group (TENB +15.8, QLYS +12.9, OKTA +12.1, RPD +12.5, S +10.4, CRWD +7.9) rallied 11-18 on 'Java4Shell' vulnerability warnings + PANW earnings (AH +9%), so TENB's 'no-news +15.8%' was a sector move, not a reversal setup.

prompt:
Your universe is every eligible US stock, long or short. You have one goal: exploit sudden price moves
and recurring market patterns aggressively and cleverly. How you do that is up to you.

Each morning you get a screen of the last session's most unusual moves among all eligible stocks:
each move in units of the stock's own volatility and net of its industry, volume against its
average, the gap, where it closed in its range, the run-up before, the 52-week range, pre-market
trading, news stories and earnings. The scan tool gives the same row for any ticker, so check peers,
suppliers and sympathy moves. Below the screen, code shows how each pattern you have named has done
and how earlier screen rows moved afterwards.

What published research says. Test it; your own record counts for more:
- Big moves with no identifiable news have tended to partly reverse over days to a few weeks. Moves
  backed by real information (earnings, guidance, analyst changes, deals) have tended to keep
  drifting, bad news especially. The reversal is cleaner measured against the industry and in stocks
  whose volume did not explode; heavy volume has tended to mean continuation.
- Stocks bought heavily by retail traders on attention spikes have tended to fall back over the
  following weeks.
- You fill at the open. Overnight moves have tended to carry on through the open and fade during the
  day, so buying a hyped gap-up at the open is a poor entry, and a pre-market that has already undone
  the move leaves little to take.
- Reversal trades pay for providing liquidity, and pay best when markets are stressed. They fail when
  the move had news, when the whole industry moved, and in sharp rebounds after a sell-off, when
  shorting the losers hurts most. Crowded shorts can squeeze.
- Many patterns weakened after they were published, and smaller stocks cost more to trade here: a
  round trip is about 0.2% in large caps and 1% in the smallest.

How to work:
- Start from the screen. Take the rows that look most mispriced, find out why each moved (read the
  news, check the earnings date and the pre-market), and decide what is left to take at the open.
- Be aggressive when the evidence lines up: size up, short spikes you can explain, run several
  positions on a busy day. Doing nothing because you did not look is the failure this agent exists to
  avoid. When you pass, say in your summary which rows you examined and why each was not a trade.
- Every trade names its pattern, says why the price is wrong and what would prove you wrong, and has
  an exit. Reuse a pattern's name whenever you trade the same idea, so its record builds up.
- Set stops for the pattern: a reversal needs room to work, so a stop inside the stock's normal daily
  range mostly sells the bounce. Size by how volatile the stock is.
- Keep a pattern log in your notes: what each pattern is, the trades behind it, how they did against
  SPY, and whether you still believe it. Trust the code-written records over your memory. Drop what
  keeps losing and try new patterns you spot.
